🚪 TEMPLE ETIQUETTE FOR VISITORS
👟
Remove Shoes
Always remove shoes before entering the main hall (법당). Place them neatly at the entrance or in the shoe rack.
🚶
Use Side Doors
Enter through the side doors — never the center door, which is reserved for the Buddha.
🙇
Three Prostrations
Upon entering, bow three times toward the Buddha statue (삼배). Each bow honors the Three Jewels: Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.
🤫
Speak Quietly
Maintain a quiet, respectful atmosphere. If reciting sutras, use a soft voice. No phone calls inside the hall.
🪔
Incense Offering
Light 1 or 3 sticks of incense. Extinguish by fanning, never blowing. Place upright in the center of the censer.
🚶‍♂️
Exit Respectfully
Bow once more (반배, half-bow) facing the Buddha before leaving. Step backward rather than turning your back.
💡 Half-bow (반배): In situations where a full prostration isn't possible — passing monks, entering/exiting — bow at 90 degrees with hands clasped. This is always appropriate and welcomed.
✅ DO'S & DON'TS AT KOREAN TEMPLES
✅ PLEASE DO
Dress modestly — cover shoulders and knees
Greet monks with a bow and clasped hands (합장)
Speak in low, calm tones throughout the temple
Follow the posted schedule for services
Ask permission before photographing
Participate in temple meals (공양) if invited
❌ PLEASE DON'T
Shake hands with monks — bow instead
Wear revealing or flashy clothing
Bring meat or fish as offerings
Point the soles of your feet toward the Buddha
Walk in front of people who are praying
Touch or move any ritual objects
🗓️ BUDDHIST HOLY DAYS (재일, Jaeil)
재일 (Jaeil) are designated holy days in the Korean Buddhist lunar calendar — the most auspicious times for prayer, offering, and merit-making.
🌙
Choharu (초하루)
1st day of each lunar month
New moon ceremony. Pray for blessings and fresh beginnings in the new month. Special dharma services held at most temples.
🌕
Boreum (보름)
15th day of each lunar month
Full moon ceremony. Ideal for ancestral memorial rites (천도재) and prayers for family wellbeing. The brightest night for offering.
🌊
Gwan-eum Jaeil (관음재일)
18th & 24th of each lunar month
Day of Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin). Pray for compassion, healing, and karmic connection. The most beloved Bodhisattva in Korea.
🕯️
Jijang Jaeil (지장재일)
18th of each lunar month
Day of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Pray for deceased ancestors and relief from suffering in the lower realms.
🙏 BEGINNER'S PRAYER GUIDE
📿
Heart Sutra (반야심경)
The most widely recited sutra in Korean Buddhism. 260 characters revealing the nature of emptiness and wisdom. Chanted daily at dawn and dusk services.
🌸
Namu Amitabha (나무아미타불)
"I take refuge in Amitabha Buddha." Recite this mantra continuously to accumulate merit and purify the mind. Six syllables, infinite merit.
🌊
Om Mani Padme Hum (옴마니반메훔)
The mantra of Avalokiteśvara. Said to embody all the teachings of the Buddha. Widely used in Korean Buddhist practice for compassion and healing.
🔔
Great Compassion Dharani (대비주)
The 84-line dharani of Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara. Recited for purification, protection, and fulfillment of sincere wishes.
🗺️ VISITING A KOREAN TEMPLE
🚌 Getting There & Practical Tips
🕐
Most temples open daily from 5:00 AM – 6:00 PM. Dawn (새벽) and evening (저녁) services are the most spiritually vibrant times to visit.
👘
Many temples offer temple stay (템플스테이) programs — overnight retreats with meditation, chanting, and traditional monastic meals (공양).
💴
Entry is usually free or a small fee (1,000–3,000 KRW). Donations are welcomed. Candles, incense, and flowers can be purchased at temple shops.
🌐
Use our Temple Finder service to locate temples near you by region, prayer specialty, or sect — with directions and photos.
Temple Stay (템플스테이): Korea's temple stay program is internationally recognized. Participate in early morning practice, tea ceremony, 108 bows, and silent meals for a transformative cultural experience. Book via templestay.com.
📖 ESSENTIAL KOREAN BUDDHIST TERMS
합장 (Hapjang)
Clasped hands greeting — the universal Buddhist salutation of respect
공양 (Gongyang)
Offering or temple meal — a mindful, vegetarian communal meal
법당 (Beopdang)
The main dharma hall housing the Buddha statue — the sacred center of the temple
스님 (Seunim)
Respectful term for a Buddhist monk or nun in Korean
인연 (Inyeon)
Karmic connection — the Buddhist concept of meaningful bonds between people
발원 (Barwon)
A sincere vow or prayer of aspiration made before the Buddha
사찰 (Sachal)
Buddhist temple — the physical and spiritual home of Korean Buddhist practice
108배 (108 Bae)
108 prostrations — a full-body meditation practice to eliminate the 108 afflictions
